title: Drive trouble & RAID recovery
summary: Protect data before pursuing a repair.

passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: Storage faults can appear as slow reads, missing volumes, unusual noises, or health warnings. A clicking mechanical drive may be failing, and repeated scans can increase stress on fragile hardware. Determine the value of the data and whether a verified backup exists before running repair tools. A missing drive may instead have a disconnected cable or a controller issue, so gather evidence without making unnecessary writes.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: RAID 1 mirrors data across drives, allowing an array to keep operating through some single-drive failures. RAID 0 stripes data for performance and provides no redundancy. Neither arrangement protects against every cause of data loss: accidental deletion, corruption, theft, and malware can affect the array. When an array reports a failed member, identify the exact drive through the controller’s information and the vendor procedure before replacing anything. Rebuilding can stress remaining drives, and pulling a healthy member from a degraded array can destroy availability. Verify backups and escalate uncertain recovery situations.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
